overview:
Sthānāṅga (Prakrit: Ṭhāṇaṃga, often referred to as Sthānāṅgasūtra) is one of the eleven aṅgas of the Śvetāmbara Jain canon and is traditionally counted as the third aṅga. It is regarded as an encyclopedic text that systematizes a vast range of Jain doctrinal, cosmological, ethical, and practical material through numerical classification. The title itself derives from the word "sthāna" (place, category), indicating that the work arranges "terms and things" into ordered groups—one-place, two-place, and so on—up to ten-place. In Śvetāmbara tradition, it is considered a key to understanding the wider āgama corpus because it touches all four major scriptural domains (anuyogas): narrative and ethics (dharmakathānuyoga), conduct (cāraṇānuyoga), metaphysics (dravyānuyoga), and calculation or technical analysis (karaṇānuyoga/gaṇitānuyoga).

Historically, Sthānāṅga is dated, in its earliest strata, to around the 4th–3rd century BCE, composed in Ardhamāgadhī Prakrit and transmitted orally for centuries. According to Śvetāmbara accounts, it was formally redacted and written down at the council of Valabhī in Gujarat, under the leadership of Devardhigaṇi Kṣamāśramaṇa, approximately 993 years after Mahāvīra’s nirvāṇa (traditionally placed in 466 CE). This council fixed the text as part of the surviving eleven aṅgas. The canonical language and style are terse and often highly technical, which led to the composition of extensive Sanskrit commentaries, most notably by Abhayadevasūri in the 11th century CE, to make the work intelligible to later audiences.

Structurally, the Sthānāṅgasūtra is divided into ten chapters, named numerically: eka-sthāna (one-place), dvi-sthāna (two-place), tri-sthāna (three-place), up to daśa-sthāna (ten-place). Each chapter lists doctrinal items, phenomena, or categories that fit the corresponding number. For example, the first chapter includes single entities such as the soul, the world, liberation, and unique cosmological or ethical categories; the second chapter treats dualities like sentient/non-sentient, mobile/immobile, liberated/non-liberated; later chapters move to triads, tetrads, and higher-numbered groupings. This numerical method does not merely serve as a mnemonic device; it reflects a broader Jain concern with systematic classification, combinatory analysis, and the mapping of reality into ordered sets.

Doctrinally, Sthānāṅga is especially important for its treatment of dravya (substances), tattva (fundamental principles), karma theory, cosmological geography (such as Jambūdvīpa and other regions), classifications of living beings, and gradations of spiritual development. It catalogues passions (kaṣāyas), types of knowledge and faith, forms of speech, modes of ascetic practice, and various karmic processes that lead to rebirth or liberation. Because it spans narrative, ethical, metaphysical, and technical domains, later tradition often describes it as a kind of condensed encyclopedia of Jain thought. In karaṇānuyoga terms, it is also valued for its numerical and combinatorial schemes, which influenced later Jain mathematical and cosmological literature.

From a sectarian perspective, Sthānāṅga is a Śvetāmbara canonical text; Digambara tradition does not accept the eleven aṅgas in the same way and regards them as lost in their original form. Nonetheless, many doctrinal themes found in Sthānāṅga—such as the classification of beings, karma theory, and cosmology—have parallels in Digambara sources, indicating a shared early heritage. Modern scholarship, working with critical editions and manuscript evidence, emphasizes that Sthānāṅga is composite, with layers of material reflecting different periods and pedagogical needs. Its Ardhamāgadhī prose, frequent lists, and sometimes cryptic formulations suggest that it functioned as a teaching text whose full meaning was unpacked orally by teachers and later in written commentaries.

In contemporary Jain study, Sthānāṅga remains central for those engaging deeply with the Śvetāmbara āgamas. Critical editions, translations, and commentaries allow students to trace how core Jain concepts were organized and transmitted in early canonical form. At the same time, the text’s density and technicality mean that it is rarely read in isolation by lay practitioners; instead, it is approached with guidance from teachers, commentarial literature, and modern study aids. As an aṅga, it is not treated as a standalone philosophical treatise but as part of a larger canonical network, where its numerical catalogues cross-reference and support other āgamas. For historical and doctrinal research, Sthānāṅga offers a window into how early Jain communities structured their knowledge and how later generations preserved and interpreted that structure.

primary_sources.title: Sthānāṅgasūtra (Ṭhāṇaṃga)
primary_sources.author: Traditionally attributed to Sudharmāsvāmī as canonical transmitter; individual authorship not specified
primary_sources.original_text: एगं जिवं, एगं लोयं, एगं धम्मं, एगं मोक्कं (Ardhamāgadhī, representative of eka-sthāna style)
primary_sources.transliteration: egaṃ jivaṃ, egaṃ loyaṃ, egaṃ dhammaṃ, egaṃ mokkaṃ
primary_sources.translation: One soul, one world, one dharma, one liberation.
primary_sources.notes: This line represents the kind of numerically organized listing found in the first chapter (eka-sthāna), where singular entities are catalogued. The Sthānāṅgasūtra is preserved in Ardhamāgadhī Prakrit and was canonically fixed at the Valabhī council in the 5th century CE. The text is divided into ten sthānas, each grouping items by number from one to ten, and serves as the third aṅga of the Śvetāmbara canon.

primary_sources.title: Sthānāṅgasūtra, eka-sthāna section (critical edition by Muni Jambūvijaya)
primary_sources.author: Canonical text; critical editor Muni Jambūvijaya
primary_sources.original_text: एगं णाणं, एगं दंसणं, एगं चरित्तं, एगं समायं (Ardhamāgadhī)
primary_sources.transliteration: egaṃ ṇāṇaṃ, egaṃ daṃsaṇaṃ, egaṃ carittaṃ, egaṃ samāyaṃ
primary_sources.translation: One knowledge, one faith, one conduct, one equanimity.
primary_sources.notes: This representative passage illustrates how Sthānāṅga lists core spiritual categories—knowledge (jñāna), faith (darśana), conduct (cāritra), and equanimity (sāmāyika)—within the numerical framework of the first chapter. Jambūvijaya’s critical edition, based on multiple manuscripts, is a major modern resource for studying the canonical form of the text and its Ardhamāgadhī language.

primary_sources.title: Sthānāṅgasūtra, dvi-sthāna section
primary_sources.author: Canonical text; traditional transmission
primary_sources.original_text: दुव्विहं भवं: संजिवी भवं, असंजिवी भवं (Ardhamāgadhī)
primary_sources.transliteration: duvviham bhavaṃ: saṃjivī bhavaṃ, asaṃjivī bhavaṃ
primary_sources.translation: Existence is of two kinds: living existence and non-living existence.
primary_sources.notes: This example from the second chapter (dvi-sthāna) shows the use of dual classification to distinguish sentient (jīva) and non-sentient (ajīva) modes of existence. Such dualities are central to Jain metaphysics and recur throughout the canon. The Sthānāṅgasūtra’s systematic listing of these pairs makes it an important source for understanding early doctrinal schemata.

misconceptions.myth: Sthānāṅga is only a mathematical or numerical text and has little to do with core Jain doctrine.
misconceptions.reality: While Sthānāṅga is famous for its numerical structure and is important for karaṇānuyoga and gaṇitānuyoga, it is fundamentally an encyclopedic doctrinal text. Its lists cover substances (dravya), karma theory, cosmology, ethics, ascetic practice, and spiritual development, making it central to understanding Jain philosophy in the Śvetāmbara canon.

misconceptions.myth: Sthānāṅga is accepted in the same way by all Jain sects, including Digambaras.
misconceptions.reality: Sthānāṅga is part of the Śvetāmbara canonical eleven aṅgas and is preserved and studied within that tradition. Digambara authorities generally hold that the original aṅgas were lost and do not recognize the Śvetāmbara versions as canonical in the same sense, even though many doctrinal themes overlap across sectarian lines.

misconceptions.myth: Because Sthānāṅga is an early canonical text, its meaning is always clear and self-explanatory.
misconceptions.reality: The Ardhamāgadhī prose of Sthānāṅga is often terse and technical, and many sūtras are difficult to interpret without commentarial support. Traditional Sanskrit commentaries, such as that of Abhayadevasūri, and modern critical scholarship are necessary to unpack its lists and categories. The text was likely designed to be taught and explained orally, not to function as a standalone, fully explicit treatise.
